description:
Space Apps 2025 winner: Best Local Impact-Kamloops. Now we’re going global.

At the Moon’s south pole, the Sun never rises more than 1.5 degrees. Peaks bask in near-endless light while craters hide ice in eternal darkness. We’re building the tool that shows astronauts exactly where and when to land. I’m a coder and a member of the Royal Astronomical Society of Canada. I need a presentation partner who loves space and can help design our slides, shape our story and present it. No coding needed.
summary:
We built the Lunar Landing Site Navigator, a free web app that answers one question for any spot near the Moon's south pole: if we land here on this date, will the lander have sunlight for power and Earth in view for radio contact, for how long, and what's a better choice if plans change?

Users explore a 3D Moon showing NASA's nine Artemis candidate landing regions. They zoom down to real NASA terrain, pick a spot and choose dates. The app shows plain answers, countdowns, a launch calendar, a lander's-eye view of the horizon and a side-by-side comparison of up to three spots. A best-spot finder scans a whole region in seconds and maps where conditions are best.

Everything uses real data: Sun and Earth positions from NASA JPL Horizons, and terrain from NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter. We checked our results against NASA's published lighting data and the Chandrayaan-3 landing.

This matters because at the south pole the Sun stays low and hills can block it, or block Earth, for days. A good spot keeps a lander alive. A simple mode makes this understandable for everyone, and a planner mode gives the detail.
details:
What it does and how it works

The Lunar Landing Site Navigator is a web app that helps plan where and when to land near the Moon's south pole. You start with a live 3D Moon showing NASA's nine Artemis candidate landing regions. You choose a region, zoom down to its real terrain, then click a spot or type its coordinates and pick your mission dates.

For that spot, the app works out the skyline: the hills and crater rims a lander would see around it. It then steps through the mission every 10 minutes and checks whether the Sun is above that skyline (power) and whether Earth is (radio contact). The results come back as plain answers:

- how much of the time the spot has sunlight and Earth in view

- the longest dark stretch and the longest time without contact

- countdowns to the next sunrise, sunset or loss of contact

- a launch calendar that marks good and poor days

- a lander's-eye view of the horizon

A best-spot finder uses the computer's graphics chip to test the whole region: almost 188 million lines of sight in about five seconds. It skips ground steeper than 8°, a slope limit published for NASA's crewed lander, and shows a map of the best spots. A compare page puts up to three spots side by side.

Benefits

- Quick comparisons for planners. Pick any spot in NASA's nine Artemis candidate regions, either by clicking or by typing exact coordinates. Compare up to three spots side by side, with the better value marked on each row, so you can judge trade-offs quickly.

- Shows what a schedule change does. Change the landing date and every answer updates straight away. A launch calendar marks each day of the month as good, fair or poor. If a date slips or hardware is late, a team can see at once whether the same spot still works or which nearby spot is better.

- The key numbers, up front. The app shows:

- how high the Sun is above the horizon, which matters for solar power

- how much of the mission has sunlight and how much has Earth in view

- the longest dark stretch and the longest time without radio contact

- live countdowns to the next sunset and Earthset

- Finds good spots for you. The best-spot finder tests a whole region in about five seconds. It leaves out ground too steep to land on and maps where sunlight and Earth contact are best.

- Works for every level. Simple mode gives plain answers and glossary tips for students and the public. Planner mode shows exact angles, times and coordinates. Both run in any web browser, including on phones, with no install.

- Answers you can trust. Everything uses real NASA data: JPL Horizons for the Sun and Earth, and LOLA for terrain. We checked the results against NASA's own lighting data and against real landings (IM-2 and Chandrayaan-3).

Intended impact

We want students, the public and early-stage mission planners to see why landing-site choice matters. At the pole the Sun stays low, so one hill can cut a lander's power or its link to Earth for days. We hope the app helps people understand Artemis and the landers that will follow.

Tools we used

- Code: TypeScript and Python.

- Website: Next.js and React. 3D is drawn with three.js through React Three Fiber, using WebGL for the graphics-chip calculations. Zustand handles app state and Tailwind CSS the styling.

- Data processing: Python scripts prepare the NASA data in advance.

- Hosting: Vercel.

- Data: Sun and Earth positions from NASA JPL Horizons, and terrain from NASA's Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter (LOLA) on the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter.

- Hardware: no special hardware. Everything ran on ordinary laptops, and the app runs entirely in the user's browser.

How it's creative

- Several ways to see the same answer. A live 3D Moon, real 3D terrain you can fly down to, a lander's-eye view of the horizon, timelines, a calendar and a colour map of best spots. Each one shows how the site, the Sun and Earth relate.

- Stand where the lander stands. Eye-level view shows the real skyline with the Sun and Earth moving along it. You can see a hill hide the Sun or Earth sink behind a crater rim.

- It shows why small changes matter. Moving a spot a short distance, or the date a few days, can turn a good spot into a poor one, and the map and calendar make that visible. You can also see how odd the Moon is: the Sun creeps along the horizon instead of rising high, and Earth barely moves in the sky.

- Real terrain, no air. The Moon has no air to bend light, so the horizon is set only by the hills around you and the curve of the Moon. The app calculates exactly that from NASA's laser height maps. It also follows the Moon's slow wobble (libration), which makes Earth rise and set over about 27 days.

- Heavy calculations, done instantly in the browser. The search uses the computer's graphics chip to test almost 188 million lines of sight in seconds, so anyone can try "what if" choices live.

Factors we considered

- Accuracy: we use only real data and checked the app against outside sources. Sun and Earth positions match JPL Horizons to within 0.004°. Sunlight results match NASA's published lighting data to within about 0.4 percentage points. We also replayed the Chandrayaan-3 landing and matched its real Sun angle at touchdown.

- Honesty: anything we drew or chose ourselves, such as the Sun's surface pattern or the slope limit, is labelled in the app.

- Ease of use: plain language, glossary tips and a layout that works on phones.

- Caution: we count Earth as "in view" only when its centre is above the skyline.

- Mission relevance: we use NASA's official candidate regions for the Artemis crewed landing.
